method: Questions were researched with an evidence-only retrieval tool over one corpus of open-access and public-domain texts (see corpus.json). Each excerpt was checked word for word against the corpus passage it cites when this file was written; corpus_chunk numbers that passage in the corpus snapshot of 2026-10-01.
questions: Where did Toulmin's model come from?
How do Toulmin's warrants and rebuttals relate to defeasible reasoning and defeaters?
What is natural language deductivism, and how does it compare with Toulmin's model?

evidence.excerpt: Hart pointed out that judges must take into account exceptional circumstances in which a legal principle cannot be applied at all or must be applied in a weakened form.
Hart refers explicitly to conditions that can defeat (Hart 1951, p. 175) the claim that a contract exists, even when the standard definition of ‘contract’ is satisfied.
Toulmin, building on Hart’s observations, argues for the importance of distinguishing between warrants and rebuttals

rebutting defeaters (which give one a prima facie reason for believing the denial of the original conclusion) and undercutting defeaters (which give one a reason for doubting that the usual relationship between the premises and the conclusion hold in the given case)
a judge is required to make a judgment on the basis of an incomplete set of facts: those facts that are presented to the judge by the two parties as germane to the claim
Toulmin’s The Uses of Argument (1958/2003) and Hamblin’s Fallacies (1970) have become theoretical touchstones

a premise, inference, and conclusion conception of argument; the notion that a good argument has premises which are true (or epistemically acceptable in some way) and a conclusion which follows from them
Typically, this implicit premise is an “associated” conditional of the form “If P, then C” where P is the argument’s premises and C is its conclusion.
Implicit Premise: If Dr. Oz says this, it must be true.
this makes it a valid argument with a problematic implicit premise
deductive validity ensuring only that the conclusion of an argument is as likely true (and certain) as its premises
Walton, Reed and Macagno 2008 provide a compendium of 96 schemes.
Other schemes that play a prominent role in real-life arguing include Argument by Sign, Argument by Analogy, Argument by Example, and Slippery Slope Reasoning.
The most common approach to argument schemes combines a pattern of argument with a set of “critical questions” with which it is associated.
